newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: DBS Land net up, but below expectations.
newsitem.headline: DBS Land net up, but below expectations.

text.p: DBS Land Ltd's net profit in the first half of 1997 expanded 12.8 percent to Singapore $113.46 million (US$75.14 million), but it fell below analysts expectations of over 20 percent growth.
"We're happy with what we did. It's a soft (property) market," DBS Land Deputy Chairman Han Cheng Fong told reporters after the results were presented in Singapore on Saturday.
"The market, over the next 12 months, will continue to be soft. I don't see people rushing to buy," Han said.
Analysts had said they expected DBS Land, the property arm of the DBS Bank group, to post growth of more than 20 percent in the first half due mainly to higher earnings from its overseas projects.
But the soft property market in Singapore, which forms the overwhelming bulk of the firm's revenues, clearly offset any gains in earnings from overseas investments.
ING Barings Securities analyst Lim Chung Chun said he was trimming his original forecast of 23 percent growth in 1997 for DBS Land to 21 percent while saying the company should bounce back.
"We expect a better second half," he said. "They have some overseas contributions kicking in."
Company secretary Lim Joke Mui said in a statement accompanying the results that DBS Land expected "to maintain the first year's operating results in the second half".
DBS Land general manager Fan Kow Hin said growth should be stronger in the rest of 1997 and projects in China and Hong Kong would contribute substantially to company earnings.
Earnings from Australia, through its unit of Australand, should also help the company.
"We believe that our portfolio will be able to sustain growth for the group notwithstanding the weak Singapore market," Fan said.

DBS Land will be launching a number of residential projects in Singapore, Hong Kong and Shanghai this year. Two hotels in Cambodia, recently hit by fighting between the country's feuding premiers, are also expected to open towards the end of 1997.
"Increasingly, we are getting more profits from overseas operations," Lim said.
